title: Rabies Risk Exposes Gaps in Vietnam’s Unregulated Dog Trade
excerpt: Rabies becomes virtually 100% fatal after symptoms appear. Uninspected slaughter and covert transport create preventable safety gaps that demand abolition by 2030.
body_html:
Once rabies symptoms appear, survival is virtually impossible. WHO identifies rabies as virtually 100% fatal after clinical symptoms develop; after a possible bite or saliva exposure, wounds need washing with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, followed by urgent medical assessment and post-exposure prophylaxis before symptoms begin. That danger stands beside food-safety warnings about unregulated slaughter and contamination risks. Families deserve protection from both.

“Tradition” cannot replace inspection

Tradition does not guarantee quarantine, traceability, veterinary inspection, or hygienic slaughter. Informal supply chains can move animals outside controlled systems, leaving authorities with weaker ability to verify origin, health status, transport conditions, or meat safety. Claims that animals are “farm-raised” require records: registered facilities, movement documents, quarantine controls, and inspection. Without those records, claim becomes marketing—not proof.

Stolen companions are not livestock paperwork

Pet theft and commercial supply chains represent a separate but connected moral and regulatory failure: animals regarded as family can disappear into networks built for profit. Every unverified origin claim shields that possibility from scrutiny. Anger belongs with thieves, illicit traders, and systems that allow animals to move without reliable oversight—not with Vietnamese families defending their pets, health, and communities.

Health protection needs action before exposure

Rabies risk usually involves infected saliva entering through bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. Uninspected handling, sick animals, and bite incidents create different exposure concerns and must not be falsely merged. Salmonella and E. coli contamination risks at informal slaughter points likewise demand inspection and enforcement. Public-health targets and enforcement measures cannot close every gap while this trade remains difficult to trace.

Vietnamese communities can lead reform that protects children, families, workers, and companion animals. SDE calls for complete national abolition by 2030—not a promise of instant closure, but a clear public demand that lawmakers and authorities can act on. Sign the national petition. Add your name, then follow campaign updates as that demand reaches decision-makers.

telegram_message:
Rabies leaves no room for unverified animal supply chains.

• WHO: rabies is virtually 100% fatal once clinical symptoms appear.
• After possible exposure: wash wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes; seek urgent medical care for vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies.
• Vietnam health and food-safety warnings identify risks linked to unregulated dog-meat consumption, including rabies pathways and contamination at informal slaughter points.
• “Farm-raised” claims need records: origin, quarantine, transport, and inspection.
• Pet theft and commercial trade are separate facts, but both expose failures in traceability and protection.

Lawful food activity, regulatory breaches, criminal theft, and SDE’s proposed abolition must remain distinct. Public safety needs enforceable reform, not slogans.

facebook_post:
Rabies control cannot stop at household gates. Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. After possible exposure, immediate washing with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and urgent medical care can save a life before symptoms begin.

Vietnamese families also face food-safety questions when animals move through informal channels. Health warnings identify risks involving rabies exposure, E. coli contamination, and Salmonella at unregulated slaughter points. These risks do not prove that every animal in the trade carries disease. They prove something narrower and harder to dismiss: without reliable origin records, quarantine, transport controls, and inspection, communities cannot verify safety.

“Farm-raised” is not evidence without documentation. Pet theft is not tradition. Criminal networks that steal companion animals and profit from weak oversight deserve scrutiny; Vietnamese communities defending family safety and animal welfare deserve solidarity.

SDE calls for complete abolition of the dog-meat trade by 2030. Sign the petition and add your voice to a public demand for enforceable reform:
